title: Unit – 5 : Session – 4 : SLO – 1  |  BFS Vs DFS
sections: I. Complete the Pseudocode — DFS (using stack)
1. Initialize an empty STACK
2. Mark all vertices as UNVISITED
3. Push the starting vertex onto the stack
4. While the stack is not empty:
a. Pop a vertex from the stack
b. If the vertex is UNVISITED:
i. Mark it as visited
ii. Push all its ADJACENT vertices onto the stack
II. Complete the Pseudocode — BFS (using queue)
1. Initialize an empty QUEUE
2. Mark all vertices as UNVISITED
3. Enqueue the starting vertex
4. While the queue is not empty:
a. Dequeue a vertex from the queue
b. If the vertex is UNVISITED:
i. Mark it as visited
ii. Enqueue all its ADJACENT vertices
III. Arrange the Steps in Correct Order
DFS: b -> c -> f -> a -> e -> d
(mark start unvisited; push start; while stack not empty: pop; mark visited; push adjacent unvisited)
BFS: b -> a -> f -> c -> d -> e
(mark start unvisited; enqueue start; while queue not empty: dequeue; mark visited; enqueue adjacent)
IV. Spot the Error
Error: the snippet uses a QUEUE with push/dequeue/enqueue — that is BFS logic, not DFS.
Correct it to: use a STACK — 1. Push starting vertex onto STACK; 2. While stack is not empty:
a. POP a vertex; b. If unvisited: mark as visited; PUSH all adjacent vertices.
V. Reasoning Activity
Use BFS. BFS explores the graph level by level from Person A, so the first time Person B is reached,
the path found has the smallest number of hops. DFS may wander deep along one branch and would not
guarantee the shortest connection.
